content.title: About
content.content: Atole is a traditional Mexican beverage made from corn masa, water, sugar, and aromatic additions such as cinnamon, vanilla, or chocolate. It is nourishing, mildly sweet, and warming, often served hot on chilly days.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Atole has ancient roots in pre‑Columbian Mesoamerican cultures.
There are many regional variations, from classic corn to chocolate (atole de chocolate) and vanilla‑flavored versions.
Traditionally the drink is prepared in clay pots, which impart a distinctive flavor.
In some regions atole is a symbol of hospitality and is served during celebrations.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Corn masa provides slow‑releasing energy, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B3, and B6 support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Atole supplies magnesium, iron, and phosphorus, important for bones and muscles.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: A warm drink helps maintain fluid balance, especially in cold weather.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Traditional atole is often sweet; people with diabetes should monitor portions or use sugar substitutes.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Added sugar and milk can make the beverage relatively high in calories.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Atole is served hot in mugs. It can be enjoyed on its own, added to desserts, used as a base for cocktails, or paired with baked goods.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry corn masa in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Prepared atole is best consumed within 24 hours; leftover drink can be refrigerated for up to 2 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Bread is a baked product made from dough consisting of flour, water, yeast (or sourdough starter) and salt. It is one of the oldest and most widely consumed foods, present in cultures around the world. Different types of flour, leavening methods and shaping produce a vast array of breads with varying flavors, aromas and textures.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first breads were baked more than 14,000 years ago in the Near East.
There are over 300 different varieties of bread, from whole‑grain loaves to baguettes and ciabatta.
Traditional sourdough contains live lactic‑acid bacteria and yeasts that enhance flavor and extend shelf life.
Bread is often called a “universal” food: it can be eaten plain, used for sandwiches, or as crumbs and breadcrumbs in cooking.
In many cultures bread symbolizes hospitality and prosperity.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Bread provides slowly digestible carbs that supply steady energy and help maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber (especially whole‑grain)
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety and contributes to gut health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B2, B3 and folate are involved in metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Bread supplies iron, magnesium, zinc and selenium, essential for immunity and metabolic processes.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota (sourdough)
items.content: Sourdough fermentation can foster beneficial bacteria in the intestine.

items.title: Gluten intolerance
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity may experience inflammation and discomfort after eating regular bread.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White bread raises blood sugar quickly, which can be problematic for diabetics.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Some breads contain high amounts of salt, which may be an issue for hypertension.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Industrial bakery products may include flavor enhancers and preservatives that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bread can be enjoyed fresh, toasted, as sandwiches, in toast, croutons, breadcrumbs, or in soups. It pairs well with butter, cheese, vegetables, cold cuts and spreads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bread in a cool, dry place in a paper bag or bread box. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag and thaw at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Coffee cake is a moist, tender cake flavored with ground coffee and often topped with a cream cheese or chocolate glaze. Made with yeast type 2439, it rises during baking, giving it a light, airy crumb. It is commonly served for breakfast, as a snack, or as a dessert with tea.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Coffee cake is a staple in many cafés as a lighter alternative to richer desserts.
Yeast type 2439 is selected for sweet doughs, providing consistent rise and a soft texture.
Ground coffee not only adds aroma but also enhances the flavor of chocolate glazes.
In some regions the cake is decorated with nuts, berries, or caramel crumbs.
A gluten‑free version can be made by substituting wheat flour with a gluten‑free blend.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Coffee contains polyphenols that help combat free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, increasing alertness and concentration.

items.title: Probiotic‑like properties of yeast
items.content: Live yeast can support gut microbiota, although it is usually killed during baking.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast provides B1, B2, B3, and B6 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Coffee cake offers plant protein from flour and yeast, contributing to satiety.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: People sensitive to caffeine may experience nervousness, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Coffee cake is often sweet; excessive sugar intake can lead to weight gain and tooth decay.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, making the cake unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: If the cake is topped with nuts, potential allergic reactions must be considered.

items.title: Yeast temperature shock
items.content: Overly hot ingredients can kill the yeast, resulting in poor rise.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve coffee cake warm or at room temperature, often alongside a cup of coffee or tea. Slice into portions, drizzle with extra glaze, add berries or whipped cream. It pairs well with ice cream, yogurt, or fruit sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cake in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. Refrigerate for up to 5 days for longer freshness. Freeze in freezer‑safe bags for up to 2 months; thaw at room temperature before serving.

ham-or-pork-noodles-and-vegetables-inclu.title: Ham or pork with noodles and vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of ham or lean pork, boiled noodles, and vegetables (carrots, broccoli and/or dark‑green leafy greens). It is served without sauce, preserving the natural flavors of the ingredients and keeping added fat low.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ham is traditionally made from the hind leg of a pig, while lean pork cuts such as loin are lower in fat.
Wheat noodles provide a quick source of carbohydrates, delivering energy for active lifestyles.
Broccoli is rich in vitamin C and compounds that support the body’s detoxification processes.
Carrots contain beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A, essential for vision.
Dark‑green leafy vegetables (spinach, kale) are excellent sources of iron and folate.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Ham and lean pork supply high‑quality animal protein needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: Pork provides vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Broccoli and leafy greens are loaded with vitamin C and antioxidants that help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Leafy greens and broccoli deliver calcium and vitamin K, supporting bone mineralization.

items.title: Blood‑sugar regulation
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables and noodles slows glucose absorption, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ham is often cured and salty, so people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Some pork cuts can be higher in saturated fat, which may be a concern for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an allergic reaction to pork.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked pork can harbor pathogens; ensure internal temperature reaches at least 71 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, mixing sliced ham or pork pieces with boiled noodles and lightly sautéed vegetables. Optionally garnish with fresh herbs or a squeeze of lemon juice for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared meal in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 2 months. Thaw in the fridge and reheat until piping hot.

potato-from-puerto-rican-chicken-fricass.title: Potato from Puerto Rican chicken fricassee, with sauce

content.title: About
content.content: This dish features boiled or roasted potatoes served in a fragrant sauce made from slow‑cooked Puerto Rican‑style chicken. The chicken is simmered with tomatoes, bell pepper, garlic, olive oil and spices, then the sauce is combined with the potatoes, creating a rich, slightly spicy flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Puerto Rican cuisine blends Spanish, African and Indigenous influences.
Traditional fricassee is cooked in a single pot, allowing flavors to meld together.
Young, waxy potatoes are often used so they hold their shape during long simmering.
The sauce is sometimes enriched with coconut milk or cream for a silky texture.
The dish is commonly served with rice, beans or crusty bread to soak up the sauce.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meal supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and folate, supporting metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which helps regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and bell pepper add lycopene and vitamin C, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Olive oil and, when used, coconut milk contribute monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to poultry, experiencing skin reactions or digestive issues.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the sauce is prepared with a lot of salt or commercial broth, sodium levels can be high.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Adding cream or coconut milk increases calories, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Potential pathogens
items.content: Chicken must be cooked thoroughly to avoid salmonella and campylobacter infections.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, garnished with fresh herbs such as parsley or cilantro. It pairs well with boiled rice, quinoa or whole‑grain bread that can soak up the sauce. A squeeze of lime or a dash of hot sauce can brighten the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When reheating, add a splash of water or broth to keep the sauce from becoming too thick.

rice-white-cooked-made-with-margarine.title: Rice, white, cooked, made with margarine

content.title: About
content.content: White rice, cooked and prepared with margarine, is a ready‑to‑eat side dish. The margarine gives it a smooth texture and a subtle buttery flavor, as well as a modest amount of fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is the most widely consumed type of rice worldwide.
Cooking with margarine raises the calorie count compared with plain boiled rice.
Margarine is often used as a butter substitute in cooking because it is cheaper.
Rice readily absorbs the flavor and aroma of added fats, making the dish richer.
In many cultures, rice with butter or margarine is a traditional accompaniment to meat dishes.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides a quick source of carbohydrates, while margarine adds extra calories from fat.

items.title: Source of vitamin B1
items.content: White rice contains thiamine, important for carbohydrate metabolism and nerve function.

items.title: Easy digestion
items.content: Soft, cooked rice is gentle on the stomach and suitable for diets requiring bland foods.

items.title: Fatty acids
items.content: Margarine may contain vegetable oils rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids.

items.title: Reduced glycemic spikes
items.content: Combining rice with fat can slow the rise of blood sugar after a meal.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: The mix of carbs and fat makes the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: Some margarines contain trans fats, which are linked to heart disease.

items.title: Low fiber
items.content: White rice is low in dietary fiber, so it should be paired with vegetables or whole grains.

items.title: Allergy to vegetable oils
items.content: A minority of people may react to ingredients in certain margarines.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice with margarine as a side to meat, fish, or vegetable dishes. Enhance the flavor with herbs, spices, sauces, or mixed vegetables for variety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat until steaming hot before serving. Discard if left at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: A tart is an open‑topped pastry with a filling, typically made from a dough of flour, butter and eggs. Tarts can be sweet (fruit, berries, custard) or savory (vegetables, meat, cheese). The crust is often shortcrust, puff pastry or yeasted dough, and the filling is prepared separately and placed on the pre‑baked base.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tarts originated in France in the 17th century and quickly spread across Europe.
The word “tart” comes from the Old French “tarte”, meaning a flat pie.
The most famous sweet version is the Tarte Tatin, where apples are caramelised under the pastry and then flipped.
Savory tarts are commonly served as appetizers or light meals, especially in Mediterranean cuisine.
Gluten‑free tart crusts can be made using rice or almond flour.

items.title: Rich source of energy
items.content: Tarts provide carbohydrates and fats that supply quick energy.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Fruit‑filled sweet tarts deliver vitamin C, potassium and fibre, while savory versions contribute iron and calcium from cheese and meat.

items.title: Protein in savory varieties
items.content: Tarts with meat, fish or legumes are good sources of animal or plant protein.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweet tarts can contain a lot of added sugar, which is undesirable for diabetics or weight management.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Butter‑based crusts are high in saturated fats and should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Tarts often contain gluten, dairy, nuts or eggs – common allergens.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tarts can be served warm or cold. Sweet versions are often paired with whipped cream, ice cream or berry sauce. Savory tarts are sliced into portions and enjoyed with a salad or dipping sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a finished tart in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze it tightly wrapped for up to 2 months. Reheat in the oven before serving to restore a crisp crust.

yogurt-nonfat-milk-flavors-other-than-fr.title: Yogurt, nonfat milk, flavors other than fruit

content.title: About
content.content: Yogurt made from nonfat milk without fruit flavorings is a fermented dairy product created by culturing skimmed milk with live Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus. Flavors may include plain, vanilla, chocolate, caramel, etc.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Nonfat yogurt retains most of the milk protein while containing virtually no fat.
The absence of fruit flavorings makes the product more neutral, ideal for cooking and baking.
Yogurt provides live probiotic cultures that support gut health.
In many markets it is sold in 150‑ml to 500‑ml containers.
Lactose content is lower than in whole milk but not completely eliminated.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Nonfat yogurt supplies about 5 g of protein per 100 g, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Virtually no fat makes it suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: It is a good source of calcium for bone health and is often fortified with vitamin D.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Live cultures aid digestion and support the immune system.

items.title: Low added sugar (when fruit flavors are omitted)
items.content: Without fruit flavorings, the product usually contains less added sugar.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Although lactose is reduced, people with intolerance should still be cautious.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions to casein or whey can occur in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Added additives
items.content: Some brands include stabilizers or sweeteners; check labels if you have sensitivities.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy it plain, blend into smoothies, use as a base for sauces, in casseroles, or as a low‑calorie substitute for sour cream and mayonnaise.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 1‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. Do not freeze, as texture may become grainy.
